Aeschylus. The earliest of the three great Greek tragedians and a pioneer of dramatic form itself. He fought at Marathon against the Persians, witnessing the Greco-Persian Wars firsthand. This experience of warfare and civic heroism shaped his plays, which explored justice, divine will, and human suffering on a cosmic scale. Aeschylus won the dramatic competition at Athens' City Dionysia festival at least thirteen times, establishing tragedy as a serious literary form worthy of civic celebration. He pioneered the use of the second actor, expanding dramatic possibility from monologue and chorus to true dialogue and conflict; he essentially invented the confrontation as a dramatic engine. His surviving works include The Oresteia, a trilogy comprising Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides, which traces the curse on the house of Atreus across three generations. It is the only complete Greek tragedy cycle to survive. Prometheus Bound dramatizes the Titan's defiance of Zeus, making the divine tyrant himself a subject of critique and raising questions about justice and authority that persist in political philosophy. His plays feature grand, cosmic language and elaborate choral odes that emphasize fate, divine justice, and the paradox that suffering can bring wisdom—what he called learning through suffering. Aeschylus believed in the moral improvement of citizens through theater; tragedy was not mere entertainment but a civic and ethical institution. He was succeeded by Sophocles, who inherited his tragic form and refined it with psychological subtlety and irony. Euripides came after both and questioned the very premises of divine justice that Aeschylus took as cosmic law.
